questions.question: In an LWE public key b = A·s + e (mod q), what is the role of the error term e?
options: It hides the exact linear relation so recovering s becomes hard
It makes A invertible by construction for any m and n
It allows decryption to compute s by dividing b by e
It prevents any modular wrap-around from ever happening
questions.explanation: If e=0, (A,b) is just linear equations; small error keeps structure but makes recovering s hard at the right dimensions.

questions.question: What is the main reason real systems use hybrid encryption (KEM-DEM) instead of encrypting long messages directly with public-key math?
options: Public-key operations are expensive/large; symmetric encryption is fast and compact
Public-key encryption cannot be randomized, so it leaks repeated messages
Symmetric encryption is always information-theoretically secure
Hybrid encryption removes the need for randomness entirely
questions.explanation: KEM-DEM uses public-key crypto to protect a small key, then uses symmetric crypto for the bulk data efficiently.

questions.question: In toy Regev encryption, what is the public key and what is the secret key?
options: Public key is (A, b) and secret key is s
Public key is (s, e) and secret key is (A, b)
Public key is A only and secret key is b
Public key is (A, s) and secret key is e
questions.explanation: The public key is an LWE instance (A, b=A·s+e mod q); the secret key is the hidden vector s.

questions.question: In encryption, what is the conceptual purpose of choosing r ∈ {0,1}^m?
options: It selects a random subset/combination of the published equations
It makes the matrix A orthogonal over Z_q
It deterministically derives the secret key from the public key
It forces the error terms to cancel out to exactly zero
questions.explanation: The binary vector r forms a random linear combination of rows; this is what produces u=A^T·r (plus small noise).

questions.question: Why does encryption add μ·(q/2) to v (mod q) in the bit scheme?
options: It encodes the bit as a value far from 0 so small noise won’t confuse it
It ensures v is always the same for μ=0 and μ=1
It guarantees the secret s becomes uniform in Z_q^n
It makes the scheme deterministic (no randomness needed)
questions.explanation: Using two well-separated targets (0 and q/2) lets decryption decide which one the phase is closer to despite noise.

questions.question: Decryption computes x = v - <u, s> (mod q). In the small-noise case, x should be closest to what values?
options: 0 when μ=0, and q/2 when μ=1
A uniformly random value in {0,…,q−1} regardless of μ
The determinant of A when μ=0, and 0 when μ=1
Always exactly 0 if the implementation is correct
questions.explanation: After removing the structured part, only the encoding term μ·(q/2) and small noise remain.

questions.question: Which failure mode is most directly responsible for bit flips when q is chosen too small?
options: Noise wraps around modulo q so the phase can land closer to the wrong target
The secret vector s becomes all zeros with high probability
The ciphertext becomes identical for μ=0 and μ=1
The RNG produces negative numbers, which Python cannot represent
questions.explanation: If the phase crosses the midpoint due to modular wrap-around, the circular-distance test can misclassify the bit.

questions.question: Attack-themed: why do toy parameters make brute-force recovery of the secret s feasible?
options: The secret space is tiny (e.g., ternary vectors) so enumeration is possible
LWE becomes easy as soon as q is prime
Using a matrix A with m>n always reveals s immediately
The encryption step leaks s directly in u
questions.explanation: With small n and small secret distributions, you can enumerate candidates and check whether the implied errors stay within the bound.
